text: This is the command every stage and file format exist to serve. COPY INTO reads from a stage, applies a file format, and writes rows into a real table.
After it runs, Query History shows exactly what happened — a real duration and profile, not an estimate you have to trust blindly.
COPY INTO doesn't run for free. It needs a virtual warehouse to do the work, and this is where you'd resize or suspend the one it used.
Size the warehouse up and the same load finishes faster — one dropdown, and you're trading more credits per hour for less wall-clock time.

Here's the surprise for anyone coming from SQL Server: Snowflake remembers what it already loaded. It tracks every loaded file by name and checksum for 64 days, so re-running the same COPY INTO skips files it already saw — unless you set FORCE equals TRUE to reload them anyway.
Put together, one statement names the stage, the file format, and the target table, with a pattern to filter files and an ON_ERROR clause to decide how forgiving to be.
Next: loading from cloud storage you already own — the same COPY INTO, pointed at your own S3, Azure, or GCS bucket.
